items.prompt: Why were dodo eggs, laid in a nest on the ground, so vulnerable once pigs and rats arrived on the island with sailors?

options.label: The eggshell was too thin to survive being touched
options.feedback: Shell thickness was not unusual for a ground-nesting bird its size; the danger came from what could reach the egg, not from a fragile shell.

options.label: The nest was built high in trees, easy for climbing rats to reach
options.feedback: The nest sat on the ground, not in a tree; height was not the vulnerability here.

options.label: The nest sat in the open on the ground, and the dodo had never had to defend eggs from a ground predator
options.feedback: Raised on an island with no mammal predators before, the dodo had no defensive behaviour against an animal walking up to a ground nest, and pigs and rats simply ate what they found there.

options.label: The dodo laid its eggs directly in seawater
options.feedback: Eggs laid in water would not survive at all; the nest sat on dry ground, not in the sea.

items.ok_line: An island where nothing had ever come for an egg on the ground.
items.ko_line: Think about what predator this bird had ever had to defend an egg against, before people arrived.
items.exp_title: No instinct for a threat that had never existed
items.exp_text: On an island with no land mammals before people arrived, nothing had ever threatened a dodo's egg from the ground, so the birds had never evolved any defensive behaviour against that kind of danger. When pigs and rats came ashore with passing ships, they found nests sitting undefended in the open, with eggs the birds made no attempt to guard against an unfamiliar kind of threat. A defence built for one set of dangers over a long span of time offered nothing at all against a threat that had never existed before.

items.prompt: Even after intense hunting stopped, why couldn't the remaining passenger pigeons recover their numbers?

options.label: They depended on enormous flocks to nest and breed successfully, and small groups could not do so
options.feedback: Breeding success depended on the sheer size of the nesting colony itself — as flocks shrank below that scale, breeding largely failed even though hunting pressure had eased.

options.label: A new disease appeared and wiped out the last survivors
options.feedback: No epidemic disease is recorded as the cause here; the failure to recover traces instead to the birds' own breeding habits once flocks grew small.

options.label: The birds forgot how to migrate without a large flock to follow
options.feedback: Migration itself was not the barrier; the failure showed up specifically in nesting and breeding once colonies grew small.

options.label: Their eggs stopped hatching due to pollution in the water they drank
options.feedback: No evidence points to pollution as the cause; the collapse in numbers is explained by breeding failure in small flocks, not by contaminated water.

items.ok_line: A breeding trigger that needed a crowd to switch on at all.
items.ko_line: Hunting had already stopped; think about what a shrunken flock itself could no longer do.
items.exp_title: A breeding habit that needed a crowd
items.exp_text: Passenger pigeons nested in colonies so large that a single one could stretch across a wide area, and that scale itself seems to have played a part in successful breeding, whether by overwhelming predators with sheer numbers or by triggering the birds' own readiness to nest. Once hunting had thinned the population down to scattered, much smaller groups, that same trigger seems to have failed to switch on, and nesting attempts collapsed even without any hunter in sight. A species whose breeding depended on the presence of a crowd could not simply start over in ones and twos.

items.prompt: What was unusual about how far a thylacine could open its jaw, compared with most meat-eating mammals its size?

options.label: It could not open its jaw at all without breaking bone
options.feedback: The jaw joint worked like that of any mammal, opening and closing without injury; the unusual trait was how far it could open, not whether it could open safely at all.

options.label: Its jaw opened only slightly, less than most cats
options.feedback: The opposite was true: the gape was unusually wide, not restricted, compared with similarly sized meat-eating mammals.

options.label: Its jaw locked shut and could not be reopened once closed
options.feedback: The jaw opened and closed freely throughout the animal's life; nothing about its joint locked it shut.

options.label: Its jaw opened far wider than that of most mammals its size
options.feedback: A hinge built with an unusually loose range of motion let the jaw swing open much further than a similarly sized cat or dog could manage.

items.ok_line: A hinge built to swing open far wider than a cat's or a dog's.
items.ko_line: Compare the joint itself, not the size of the animal.
items.exp_title: A hinge built for an unusually wide swing
items.exp_text: The joint connecting a thylacine's lower jaw to its skull was shaped to allow an unusually large range of motion, letting the jaw swing open far past the angle a cat or dog of similar size could reach. A wider gape like this let the animal take a bigger mouthful in a single bite, useful for gripping bulky prey or delivering a bite across a wider target than a narrower jaw could manage. This same loose, wide-opening joint shows up clearly in the skull, long after the muscle and skin that once worked it are gone.

items.prompt: Why couldn't a great auk simply fly away from hunters approaching its nesting colony on land?

options.label: It could fly, but only very short distances over water
options.feedback: The bird could not fly at all, over any distance; its wings had changed shape for an entirely different purpose.

options.label: Its wings had become small, flipper-like paddles built for swimming, not flight
options.feedback: Generations of diving for fish in cold northern waters had reshaped the wings into small, stiff paddles, excellent underwater but no longer capable of lifting the bird into the air.

options.label: It was too heavy from stored fat to lift off the ground
options.feedback: Stored fat helped it survive cold water, but the deeper reason it could not fly lay in the shape of the wings themselves, not simply their weight.

options.label: It refused to fly out of loyalty to its nesting partner
options.feedback: Nothing suggests the bird chose to stay; its wings were physically no longer built for flight at all.

items.ok_line: Wings traded for paddles, the same trade penguins made independently.
items.ko_line: Look at the shape of the wing itself, not at the bird's weight or its will.
items.exp_text: A great auk's wings were short, stiff, and narrow, a shape that worked as an efficient paddle for chasing fish underwater but produced nowhere near enough lift to carry the bird into the air. That same trade-off, sacrificing flight for a wing built purely for swimming, appears again independently in penguins on the far side of the world. On land, where those short paddling wings gave the bird no way to escape upward, it could do little but waddle away from anything approaching its nesting site.

items.prompt: Why couldn't a Steller's sea cow simply dive away from hunters, the way many other sea mammals can?

options.label: It had no tail to push itself downward
options.feedback: It had a broad, whale-like tail fluke well able to push it forward; the difficulty lay elsewhere, in how easily its body sank at all.

options.label: It preferred to stay near shore rather than in open water
options.feedback: Staying near shore came from feeding on shallow kelp beds, not from an inability to dive; the deeper problem was how buoyant its body was.

options.label: A thick layer of blubber made it so buoyant that it could barely submerge
options.feedback: A thick layer of blubber, needed to survive in cold northern water, also made the body so buoyant that diving deep and staying under took far more effort than surfacing did, leaving the animal feeding mostly at the surface within easy reach.

options.label: It could not hold its breath for more than a few seconds
options.feedback: Breath-holding ability was not unusually limited for a marine mammal; buoyancy, not lung capacity, kept it mostly at the surface.

items.ok_line: Too buoyant to disappear the way a diving animal needs to.
items.ko_line: Think about what the same blubber that kept it warm also did to how easily it floated.
items.exp_text: A thick layer of blubber insulated the body against cold northern water, but that same fat layer also made the body highly buoyant, floating upward the way a cork does rather than sinking easily. Diving and staying submerged took real, sustained effort against that buoyancy, so the animal spent most of its time feeding on kelp at or just below the surface instead of down in deeper water. A body built to float this readily could not simply vanish underwater the way a sleeker, less buoyant sea mammal could.

items.prompt: What was distinctive about a quagga's stripes compared with those of other plains zebras?

options.label: Stripes covered the front half of the body but faded out toward the rear, which was plain brown
options.feedback: Clear black-and-white striping across the head, neck, and shoulders gradually thinned out and disappeared toward the hindquarters, leaving the rear half of the body a plain brown coat with no pattern on it at all.

options.label: Stripes covered the whole body but were bright orange instead of black
options.feedback: The colouring involved black stripes fading into brown, not any shift toward orange anywhere on the coat.

options.label: Stripes ran vertically on the legs only, with none on the body
options.feedback: The distinctive pattern was about stripes fading from front to back across the whole body, not about stripes being limited to the legs.

options.label: The coat had spots instead of stripes anywhere on the body
options.feedback: The coat kept a striped pattern, at least toward the front of the body; no part of it carried spots.

items.ok_line: Striped up front, plain brown by the time the pattern reached the rear.
items.ko_line: The distinctive trait was about where the stripes stopped, not their colour or their place on the legs.
items.exp_title: Stripes that faded out toward the rear
items.exp_text: A quagga's head, neck, and shoulders carried the same bold black-and-white striping seen across other plains zebras, but that pattern grew fainter moving backward along the body until it disappeared entirely. The hindquarters and legs were left a plain, unbroken brown, with no trace of striping by the time the pattern reached that far back. Coloured this way, a quagga looked at a glance like a zebra fading gradually into a plain brown horse.

items.prompt: Why were Caribbean monk seals so easy for hunters to approach on the beaches where they rested?

options.label: They were too slow-moving on land to notice anyone approaching
options.feedback: Slowness on land played some part, but the deeper cause was behavioural: the seals showed little alarm at an approaching animal in the first place.

options.label: Having no natural predators on land, they had no instinct to flee from an approaching animal
options.feedback: With no land predators in their environment before people arrived, the seals had never needed an instinct to flee from something approaching on the beach, and so simply stayed put.

options.label: They gathered only in caves too small for a hunter to enter
options.feedback: The seals hauled out in the open on beaches as much as in caves, well within easy reach of anyone who found them there.

options.label: They were unable to see anything outside the water
options.feedback: Vision worked normally both in and out of the water; the vulnerability came from behaviour, not from an inability to see.

items.ok_line: No predator on land had ever taught these seals to run.
items.ko_line: Think about what these seals had never had to fear on a beach before people arrived.
items.exp_title: No instinct built for a threat like this
items.exp_text: Resting and breeding on beaches where no land predator had ever threatened them, Caribbean monk seals had never evolved any strong instinct to flee from an animal approaching across the sand. Hunters could walk right up to a resting group, since nothing in the seals' behaviour treated an approaching land animal as a danger worth escaping. A species that had never needed to run from anything on land had no defence ready once something arrived that hunted it there.

items.prompt: Why couldn't Xerces blue butterfly caterpillars simply switch to a different plant once their coastal habitat began to be built over?

options.label: The caterpillars could fly to a new area to find food
options.feedback: Caterpillars cannot fly at all; that ability belongs only to the adult butterfly stage, long after the vulnerable feeding stage has passed.

options.label: Adult butterflies laid eggs directly onto buildings instead of plants
options.feedback: Eggs were laid on the specific host plant the caterpillars needed to eat, not on buildings or any other surface.

options.label: The caterpillars ate almost anything, so the problem lay elsewhere entirely
options.feedback: The opposite was true: the caterpillars were narrowly specialised, feeding on very few plants rather than almost anything.

options.label: The caterpillars could feed only on one particular kind of plant that grew in that habitat
options.feedback: A caterpillar's digestive system and feeding behaviour were adapted to one narrow group of host plants growing in that specific dune habitat, and it could not simply switch to whatever vegetation happened to remain nearby.

items.ok_line: One caterpillar, one plant, one habitat — and the habitat vanished.
items.ko_line: Ask how many kinds of plant this particular caterpillar could actually digest.
items.exp_title: A diet narrowed to one habitat's plant
items.exp_text: A caterpillar of this species fed on a small group of host plants that grew specifically in the coastal sand-dune habitat where the butterfly lived, and its feeding behaviour and digestion were adapted closely to that particular vegetation. When building and development replaced those dunes with streets and houses, the host plants disappeared along with the ground they grew on, and the caterpillars had no broader diet to fall back on. A specialist adapted this narrowly to one plant in one habitat had nowhere left to feed once that combination of plant and place was gone.

items.prompt: Why did a Baiji, a river dolphin living in famously muddy water, rely mainly on sound rather than eyesight to find its way and hunt?

options.label: Echolocation let it build a picture of its surroundings from returning sound, useful where murky water made sight nearly useless
options.feedback: Emitting clicks and reading the pattern of their echoes let the dolphin build a detailed picture of obstacles, fish, and open water even where sunlight barely penetrated the silt-laden water.

options.label: It had no eyes at all, so sound was its only option
options.feedback: The dolphin had small but functional eyes; the shift toward relying on sound came from how little those eyes could actually make out in the murky water, not from blindness.

options.label: Sound travelled faster underwater than light did, making it more efficient
options.feedback: Sound does not travel faster than light through water or through anything else; the advantage of echolocation here was usefulness in murky water, not speed.

options.label: It surfaced constantly to look for landmarks on the riverbank
options.feedback: Relying on surface landmarks would do little in a wide, muddy river; the dolphin instead read its surroundings through sound while submerged.

items.ok_line: A picture built from echoes, in water too murky for eyes to help.
items.ko_line: Think about what a click sent into murky water can do that a glance cannot.
items.exp_text: Silt suspended in the water cut visibility down to almost nothing a short distance away, making eyesight of little practical use for finding fish or avoiding obstacles in that particular river. A Baiji instead sent out clicks and listened to how those sounds bounced back off everything around it, building a detailed picture of its surroundings out of echoes rather than light. Hunting and navigating this way worked just as well in water too murky to see through as it did in clearer water, since the sense doing the work never depended on light.

items.prompt: How did male Pyrenean ibex most likely use their large curved horns during the mating season?

options.label: By using them to dig burrows for shelter
options.feedback: Digging is done with hooves and legs; the horns' heavy, curved build instead suits clashing against another animal's horns, not moving earth.

options.label: By using them to break open plant seeds for food
options.feedback: Horns played no role in feeding; food was gathered and chewed with the mouth and teeth, as in any goat relative.

options.label: By clashing and pushing against a rival's horns to win dominance and mating access
options.feedback: Two males squaring off would lower their heads and drive their horns together, pushing and twisting against each other until one gave way, with the winner gaining access to mate.

options.label: By using them purely for display, never actually making contact with another male
options.feedback: Worn and chipped horn tips found on fossil and museum specimens show real, repeated contact between rivals, not a bloodless display alone.

items.ok_line: A contest of push and twist, decided by strength, not by a single blow.
items.ko_line: Think about what two rival males actually did with those horns when they met.
items.exp_title: Horns locked in a contest of strength
items.exp_text: During the mating season, rival males faced off and drove their heavy, curved horns directly into each other, pushing and twisting in a contest that tested strength and stamina rather than speed. Whichever male could out-push the other and force him to break away and retreat generally won the right to mate with females nearby. Built thick and curved the way they were, a male's horns worked less as a weapon against predators than as a tool for settling contests against other males of the same species.
